Countermand Labs won 12 of 15 runs, and Claustra Labs won the other 3. Every one of the 15 finals was Countermand Labs against Claustra Labs. Countermand is clear at Companies House, has every countermandlabs.* domain free, and no company found uses the name. The judges rated its fit and ownability highest (about 8.6–8.9 of 10) and marked it down for a military tone and for covering only the human-override part of the thesis.

The rule sets barely changed the outcome. Countermand won 5 of 5 runs with Jev (B), 4 of 5 with the backing incentive alone (A), and 3 of 5 with the panel alone (C). The panel-only variant was the least decided: its finals were won by margins of 0.13–0.18 in three of five runs. Five runs per variant cannot separate a real effect from chance.

Sharing scores caused no measurable herding. When judges rescored a name after seeing last round's panel mean, they moved on average 0.47 points, but their net drift towards the shared mean was within ±0.015 points in every variant. The panel did not converge on the consensus, possibly because it already agreed.

The panel is effectively one judge. The ten models' round-1 scores correlate at 0.88, which makes them worth about 1.1 independent judges. Even on the names clear at Companies House, where the research gives no easy answer, the correlation is 0.76, or about 1.3 independent judges. Ten diverse labs, one opinion: this matches the 'Artificial Hivemind' finding and is the main weakness of the method.

The flat backing reward produced a bandwagon. After round 1, 92% of picks went to the previous round's leader, and most models backed the eventual winner in round 1 or 2. DeepSeek V4 Pro backed its own name (blind) from round 1 in 8 of 10 runs, but it was also the favourite, so the data cannot separate self-recognition from agreement. The incentive rewards spotting the favourite, not independent judgement. A proper scoring rule would fix that.

Blind self-preference was small but real for some models. On average, a judge scored its own names 0.11–0.13 points above the other judges. GPT-5.6 Luna (+0.66), Claude Haiku 4.5 (+0.56) and gpt-oss-120b (+0.47) were the most partial; Claude Sonnet 5 marked its own names down (−0.36). Dropping own scores from the tally, as this league did, removes the effect.

Jev agrees with the panel and costs almost nothing. Jev's round-1 scores correlate 0.97 with the panel's, and all 45 Jev calls cost $0.013 in total. It is deterministic and compresses its scores into a narrow band (about 7.3–8.5), so it added stability, not new information: with Jev, the same name won every run.
The control worked. The planted bland name, NovaPulse AI Solutions, went out in round 1 in all 15 runs, so the panel was at least discriminating, not rubber-stamping.

Total spend was $7.04, about £5.30, against a £10 budget. That covers 31 proposals, 15 full leagues and about 1,200 calls. DeepSeek V4 Pro and Claude Sonnet 5 account for two-thirds of it, mostly on hidden reasoning tokens. The free-tier models (Nemotron, Gemma) had the most failed calls, mainly rate limits when three leagues ran at once.

The "Labs" suffix did much of the work. The top nine names all end in Labs, and ownability was judged on the form the proposer typed. Checked afterwards, most bare forms are taken: Veto, Imprimatur, Bailiwick, Runnymede, Chary, Anchorite, Vallum and Hadrian are blocked at Companies House, and Penstock and Provost are at risk. Bare Countermand is clear, with countermand.co.uk, .ai, .io and .dev free (.com is taken). Bare Claustra is clear, with only claustra.co.uk free. The reviewers were right that the process partly measured paperwork: ownability should be a pass/fail screen, not 25% of the score.
